text: Rain fell on Qing Mao Mountain for three days. Fang Yuan wiped his blade and watched the Heavenly Sword Sect disciples file past. Sect elders did not look at him. The clan head of the Fang clan had sent him here with one rule: never speak of the old quarrel. At the gate, Elder Mo stopped him. “Hunter or disciple?” the old man asked. “Neither,” said Fang Yuan. “I am only a guest.” The elder grunted, and the heavy doors opened onto a courtyard where Heaven's light fell through cloud.

Bai was not the kind of man who rushed. He poured tea for the visitors from Cold Moon Valley and waited. “Brother Bai,” said the stranger, “your master is called Bai Ning Bing in the south, is he not?” Nobody answered. Later the same man was spoken of as Bai Ningbing by the merchants, as the Frost Lord by the guards, and simply as the Venerable by his students. They all meant one old man, who sat unmoving beside the jade cup called Spring Autumn Cicada.

The auction hall of Ten Thousand Treasures Pavilion glittered. A man in grey robes, whom everyone called Hunter Li, raised one finger. “Three hundred spirit stones for the Nine-Turn Reincarnation Pill.” The auctioneer, Madam Yu, smiled thinly. “Sold.” Outside, Hunter, as the northern merchants shortened it, stood in the rain beside his disciple Zhao Rui. Nobody guessed that the master of Floating Lantern City had once bowed to him.

Dawn at Heavenly Demon Sect. The great hall was empty except for a single figure: the Heavenly Demon, also written in older records as Tian Mo, also known to his servants as Master. “Hope you slept well,” he told the kneeling steward, Hope by courtesy, since his real name was Xi Wang. “Xi Wang, send word to the Righteous Alliance. Tell them the sword has returned.” The sword in question was named Frost Sorrow, and it hummed faintly in its sheath.

Sect rules forbid fighting on the steps, so Zhou Mu only watched. Disciples of the Azure Cloud Sect practised below. A thin boy, Joy by nickname and Yue Le by birth, dropped his wooden sword. “Careless,” said Senior Brother Ji. “Brother Ji is right,” echoed Zhou Mu. Then the sect leader descended from Lotus Peak, and everyone bowed. The Sect did not forgive laziness. “Whoever breaks the Sect's rules,” he said, “answers to me.” Nobody spoke.

In the south, Madam Ouyang ruled the river trade. In the north, another Madam Ouyang ruled the salt trade, and they were not related. Merchants joked about it. “Which Madam?” they asked. Only Ouyang Xue, the younger one, found it funny. She sat among her fans at Peony Pavilion, reading a letter from Ouyang Shan. “Ouyang Shan wants the Tide Ledger,” she said. “Then he can come for it.” The rain over Wuxi never stopped that month.

Sung Jin-woo was not in the room, but everyone spoke of him. The new recruits said Sung Jinwoo with awe; the veterans said Jinwoo-nim with irony. “Sung is only a family name,” muttered the clerk. “Sung what?” “Jin-woo.” In the corner, Hunter Baek sharpened a blade. Hope was thin that season. The Red Gate Raid would begin at dawn, led by the guild master of the Silver Crane Guild.

Kim Dokja-ssi read on the subway as always. His coworkers knew him as Mr. Kim; the readers of the old web novel knew him as Dokja. “Dokja-ssi,” called Han Sooyoung, “you missed your stop.” “I know.” She sighed. Sooyoung had written half the story herself. At the next station the doors opened onto Jamsil, and a crowd of strangers pushed in, none of them aware that the Star Stream was watching.

Joy was the receptionist at Eunhaeng Tower, and she was tired of the pun. “Joy by name, not by nature,” she told Detective Oh. Oh Sung-min only laughed. “Joy-ssi, I need the Silver Key logs.” She pulled up a dusty ledger. Neither noticed the president of the building company standing in the stairwell, listening. The elevator hummed. Somewhere below, the Third Bureau prepared a warrant.

“Professor Gong is angry,” whispered Min-ji. “Gong Tae-sik is always angry,” said her friend Yun. In the lecture hall of Seorin University, the dean was giving a speech about funding, and nobody listened. Hunter licences were on the agenda, but not in the way anyone wanted. “Tae-sik sunbae will fix it,” Yun added. Outside, cherry petals covered the steps of Dongseo Hall.

Her name was Rain, and the villagers of Cheongsan never let her forget the weather jokes. Rain Kang kept her head down. “Rain-ah, the village chief wants you.” “Which one?” There were two villages sharing the valley and so two village chiefs, though in practice only Chief Bae mattered. He held the old seal, the Jade Tiger Seal, and he did not trust anyone under sixty.

Yeo Ji-an opened her shop at six. Customers called her Ms. Yeo, Jian-ssi, or just the Baker. “One Milky Way Loaf,” said a boy. “Please.” The bell above the door rang. In the street, a black car from the Haeseong Group idled; the vice-chairman was inside, watching her through tinted glass. Ji-an wiped the counter. “Plain bread,” she said quietly, “for plain people.” It was a lie, and she knew it.

Satoru Gojo was late again. The students of Kuroi Academy had stopped counting. “Gojo-sensei is here!” someone shouted, and the class scrambled. In the staff room the principal, whom the older teachers called Gojo Satoru only when they were angry, sighed. “Which Gojo?” asked the substitute. “There are two on the register.” He pointed at the strongest sorcerer in the building, also known as the Honoured One, and then at a quiet history teacher with the same family name, Gojo Mari.

“Rain-chan! Come inside!” cried the housekeeper. Rain pulled her hood down and walked on through the market of Hoshizora Town. She was a witch, though no one knew it, and her master was Lord Aizen, an old magician. “Rain-chan,” he had said, “the Moon Pearl must reach the Order of the Silver Owl by dusk.” On the way she met Takeda-san, the baker, who handed her a warm roll. “Thank you, Takeda-san.” “Mind the rain,” he said, laughing.

Tanaka-kun was the class representative of 2-B. Tanaka Ren never said much. Another Tanaka, Tanaka Mio, sat in 2-A, and the two were constantly confused. “Which Tanaka broke the window?” the teacher asked. “Mio-chan,” said a voice. “No, Ren,” said another. At the other end of the hall stood the student council president, holding a clipboard and refusing to take sides. Behind him, the sign of Aoba High glowed in the afternoon sun.

The clan head of the Kurosawa clan and the clan head of the Shinjo clan were cousins, and so both were called uncle by half the district. “Uncle has refused,” reported Kurosawa Jin. “Which one?” “Mine.” The two houses had fought over the river since before Lord Oda unified the province. Their ancestral blades, Thunder Crane and Morning Heron, hung unused in their halls. In Edo, the shogun's envoy waited for answers.

Isekai Hunter was the title printed on Kaito's guild card. In the Guild of Seven Banners he was only Kaito-san; in the tavern he was Kai. “Kai!” called the barmaid. “Sir Kaito,” corrected a knight. The city of Elmira knew him as one man with three names. In his pack lay the Starfall Compass, bright with unused magic. Outside, the city lord was raising a toast to the heroes, and not one of them had asked Kaito.

Yui and Yuri looked alike but were not related. At Seiran Girls' School, people mistook one for the other. “Yui-senpai!” cried a first-year. “Wrong one,” said Yuri. “Yuri-senpai!” “Better.” In the library, Librarian Morita stamped returns. Heaven help the student who returned a book late. The old woman had a ledger and a memory like a trap. On the roof the two girls ate lunch beneath a sky the colour of milk, safe from the Discipline Committee.

The village headman and the temple headman of Kanchipuram shared the title Periyavar, which means elder. When Murugan arrived, he was unsure whom to greet. “Periyavar is at the river,” a boy said. “Which?” “The tall one.” Murugan touched his forehead. “Thambi,” called an old woman, “bring water.” Beyond the paddy fields rose the gopuram of the Shiva Temple, where the bronze lamp Eternal Flame had burned since before the Pallava Dynasty fell.

Grace is a word of English origin, but Grace Menon was born in Kerala. At the Holy Cross School she was Grace-miss, and at home she was Gracy. “Menon-madam, your result is out,” the clerk said. Nobody told her the principal, the Sister Superior, had already read it. In the corridor, Sister Agnes folded a paper boat. Monsoon wind pushed at the shutters of Kottayam. “Do not worry, Grace,” she said. “God has plans.”

Raj and Raja were brothers, and the second was the elder, which confused everyone. In the market of Jaipur, traders called Raja-bhai the clever one. “Raj will inherit the shop,” said their mother. “Not if the Marwari Merchants' Guild has anything to say.” The head of the guild, a stern man known only as Seth-ji, had come to collect. Beside the ledger lay the old brass lamp, Aladdin's Cousin, that the family refused to sell.

The Holi Festival Committee met at Krishna Apartments. Mr. Verma, the secretary, and another Mr. Verma, the treasurer, glared at each other across the table. “Verma-sahab,” said the chairman, “please decide which of you will speak.” Both rose. The chairman sighed and handed Tara the gavel. Tara, who was twelve and the only sensible person present, banged it. “Colours at five,” she said, and the committee obeyed without a word.

Hope Nair ran a clinic in Mysuru. Hope was her real first name, chosen by a missionary grandmother. Locals said Dr. Hope or Doctor-amma. “Amma,” called a patient's child, “mummy is sick.” The clinic, called House of Mercy, had four beds and one fan. The district collector visited once a year, and promised a grant each time. “Hope Nair,” he said now, “your clinic will be funded.” She had heard it before, and kept her notebook, The Green Ledger, in her bag.

Long ago, in the kingdom of Kalinga, two brothers shared the title Raja. The elder ruled the hills, the younger the plains. Both were called Raja by their people, and Ashoka was the only one who ever dared to ask which. Prince Ashoka was neither, and was the king's nephew. His horse, Moonrise, had no rival. At the gate of Dhauli, the old Mahamatya bowed and said, “Yuvraj, the war is lost.” Nobody argued.

Will stood at the window. Will Brandon had a habit of silence, and the household of Marlow House was used to it. “Master Will,” said the butler, Hawkins, “your uncle asks for you.” The uncle, whom the servants called the Old Squire and whom the county called Sir Edmund, was dying. Outside, a gust moved the oaks. “Say I am coming, Hawkins.” Behind him on the mantel ticked the clock Old Dutch.

Bianca Rossi hated her name on invoices, so she signed B. Rossi. In Verona the clients called her Signora Rossi and her mother, fondly, Bianchina. Another Rossi, the baker, lived across the piazza, and the mayor could never tell the two apart. “Signora Rossi,” said the courier, “which one?” She pointed at the sign: Rossi & Figli. “Not me, then.” In the window stood a cracked mirror, the Lantern Glass, priced at nothing.

Rain pattered on the roof. Rain was an odd name for an Englishman, but Rain Whitcombe had inherited it with the manor, Greywater. “Mr. Whitcombe,” said the agent, “the bank has written.” “Whitcombe will not sell.” “Sir.” The agent hesitated. “The Greywater Estate Committee asks whether you will meet them.” “Tell them the master of Greywater is at home to nobody.” In the hallway ticked Grandfather: a clock older than the house.

In the glen, two chieftains called The MacLeod disagreed. One held Dunvegan Hill; the other Glen Ardroch. Both were addressed as The MacLeod at the Highland Games, to the confusion of tourists. “MacLeod,” said the piper, Angus, “the pipes are ready.” “Which?” “Yours.” Angus was fond of ancient tunes, especially The Lament of Dunyvaig. The Clan Gathering Committee had asked him to pick something merry, and he refused with great dignity.

Sigrid rowed out at dawn. The fishermen called her Sigrid the Younger, to distinguish her from her aunt, Sigrid the Elder. Both were fierce. In the fjord village of Aurland, the Jarl ruled by custom, and the Hird Brotherhood kept his halls. “Sigrid,” said the Jarl, “your boat is late.” “The wind, my lord.” Behind them, the rune stone Odin's Eye gleamed with frost. Hope of a warm hearth kept the rowers moving.

Lena Marek stood alone at the border station of Cesky Krumlov. The officer checked her papers. “Marek. Mr. or Ms.?” “Ms. Marek.” He stamped them. In her suitcase lay the notes of Professor Havel, her teacher, and a small brass bell, The Little Bell of Prague. The Sokol Society would be waiting on the other side. “Lenka,” she whispered to herself, her mother's old pet name. Rain hit the glass of the booth. The barrier rose.

“Will you come?” asked Zaeli, and the stranger, Kor Veshtan, paused. Everyone in the harbour called him Will, because he never said no. Kor was his true name, and Veshtan his family's. Their ship, the Dusk Marten, tugged at its rope. The harbourmaster of Pellam Quay waved them off, and a flock of gulls rose over the Brass Guild warehouse. “Zaeli,” said Will, “cast off.”

A city and its first king shared one name, which caused no end of confusion. The scholars at the Library of Ashmoor wrote King Ixomir for the man and Ixomir for the place. “Archivist Pell,” said a student, “which Ixomir is in the first scroll?” “Both,” said Pell. “Neither.” The Scroll of Seven Doors smelled of dust and oil. A bell rang from the Quiet Tower, and the students gathered their notes.

Grace was a virtue in Merrowdeep, and a name as well. Grace Ilmarin bowed at the temple of the Tidal Choir. “Lady Ilmarin,” said the cantor, “the sea is calling.” “It always is.” People called her Grace, or Ilmarin, or the Pearl Matron; each meant the same patient woman. Her lantern, Mourning Star, never lit by itself. Beyond the harbour, the black kelp rolled in slow waves.

The dragon had three names. The villagers of Hollowmere said Skarn; the scholars at the Academy of Flame said Skarnathyx; the knights said the Grey Tyrant. “Which is correct?” asked Sir Aldous. “All.” In the cave mouth, a bell hung from a chain: the Bell of Ruin. The old knight-commander struck it once. A long, slow breath answered from the dark, and the villagers, far below, stopped their work and bowed.

Sentry Dovrin reported to Commander Eleth at dawn. “Eleth,” he said, “the Ninth Fleet has not returned.” The commander nodded. In the war room of Station Calyx, the map of the Veiled Sector glowed. “And the Vice-Admiral?” “Missing.” “Dovrin, send for Doctor Ishka.” The doctor arrived, carrying the Sigil of Nine Wounds, the only proof that the fleet had ever reached the Maw. Nobody liked that proof.

In the forest of Eldrasil, two druids answered to Greywalker. One was Aenwyn Thistle; the other Corvus Ash. When a lost child asked, “Greywalker, where is the road?”, both said, “Follow me.” The Circle of Moss had never resolved the problem. Aenwyn favoured the staff Rootsong; Corvus kept a horn named Thornwhisper. The child, Mina, trailed behind, delighted by the confusion and sure she was in no danger.

Hana Kim, Kim Hana, and Hana-chan were the same girl in three countries. In Seoul she was Hana-ssi; in Osaka, Kim-san; online, Starfall. “Starfall is streaming,” said a fan. The Moonlit Esports Club had signed her last winter. The coach, Coach Barros, from Sao Paulo, spoke four languages poorly. “Hana, focus.” She adjusted her headset and the match began.

The Wanderer's Inn was full of strangers. Fang Yuan drank tea beside Sir Roland, while Kiran and Aiko argued over dice. “Fang-ge,” said Aiko, “you owe me.” “Kiran-ji won.” In the corner, the innkeeper, Old Marta, counted coins and a cat named Rain slept on her lap. “Marta,” said Roland, “a room.” “All rooms taken.” The Seven Roads Guild had booked the whole floor.

Dust blew over Karakorum Camp. Temujin was only a boy then, called Temu by his mother, and Boy-with-Blue-Eyes by the older warriors. “Temujin,” said Jamukha, “the khan calls.” “Which khan?” There were two: one over the Merkit, one over the Tayichiud. Jamukha shrugged. The two boys ran across the steppe, carrying a bone token called the Eagle Knuckle, and the grass bent in waves behind them.

“Ghost,” said the pilot, “drop in.” Ghost was the callsign of Lt. Amara Osei, who had never been to Accra but whose parents were from there. The squadron, the Blue Falcons, flew from Station Delphi. Her wingman, Dev, called her Lieutenant when angry, Osei when calm. The colonel watched from the tower. “Ghost and Dev, the Silver Corridor is yours.” Engines roared, and the sky filled with light.
